doc.title: Objects and Arrays
doc.paragraph: Most of the data you work with in Adaptive Script comes in two shapes. An object holds named properties, like a person with a first name and an age. An array holds an ordered sequence of values, like a list of that person's email addresses. What you can do with them is provided by Adaptive Functions registered in the environment, rather than by methods that belong to each value.

You can still call those functions in a way that reads like a method. x->f(a) means f(x, a): the value on the left is passed as the first argument. Any function works this way, including the script functions you write yourself. That is why the value a function works on is always its first parameter, as in map(array, fn) and slice(s, 1), so that a->map(fn) reads naturally.

The method form is spelled -> rather than ., because . reads a property: o.f(x) calls the function stored in property f of o. Keeping the two apart means a property that happens to have the name of a built-in never hides it, and a misspelled function name is still reported when the script is compiled.

This page is an overview of everyday work with objects and arrays, and with strings, which you can walk much like arrays. The details of each function are in the Function Reference, under the categories object, array, and higher_order_array, and with polymorphic functions such as freeze and length.

An object is written as property names and values between braces. A property name may be an identifier, a string literal, or an expression in square brackets. An expression in brackets is evaluated when the object is, and its result, a string, is the property name. A name that is not a valid identifier, such as one with a space in it, is written as a string literal or in brackets. The same bracket form is used for obj[name] get and assignment on an existing object. A property name is always a string, so o[1] is an error rather than property "1"; write o["1"] or o[to_string(n)].

Core property helpers include property_get, property_exists, property_delete, and add_properties. Prefer property_get(obj, name, default) when a missing property should supply a default. An object or array default is yours to change: changing it does not change the default the next call gets.

Each call builds a new array, a snapshot of the names, values, or pairs at that moment, in the order the object keeps its properties. If you change the object afterward, a snapshot you already have stays as it was.
entries gives you an array of two-element arrays, [name, value], which is handy with for-of and with functions such as map and filter.

doc.paragraph: An array is an ordered sequence of values, written between square brackets, and its indexes start at zero. Every index from zero up to its length minus one holds an entry, although an entry may be undefined. An array is not a kind of object, so you walk it with for-of or with the array functions.

length returns the number of entries. The other things you do with an array, such as slice, join, reverse, sort, map, filter, find, and reduce, are ordinary Adaptive functions that take the array as their first argument, so each can also be written as a->map(fn).

section.paragraph: Between commas in an array literal you may omit a value. That position still counts toward the length and holds undefined (the same idea as writing undefined explicitly).

A trailing comma before the closing bracket does not add an extra entry: [1,] has length 1. You can leave out a value like this in Adaptive Script and in relaxed JSON, but not in JSON, where every element must have a value.
for-of and higher-order functions such as map and filter walk every index from zero through length minus one, including positions whose value is undefined.

section.header: Indexing with at and bracket form
section.paragraph: at(array, index) returns the value at a signed index. Negative indexes count from the end (-1 is the last element). Out of range yields undefined (nullish), not an error.

Bracket indexing a[index] is also zero-based but counts from the start only: a negative index, like one past the end, reads as undefined, and assigning a[-1] = v is an error. Use at(a, -1) to read from the end and a[length(a) - 1] = v or with_at(a, -1, v) to write.
These functions require a mutable array (not frozen). They modify the target in place.
push / pop form a stack (LIFO). push / shift form a queue (FIFO). Method form is available, for example a->push(4), a->pop().

Assignment to an index can also grow a mutable array by one entry when the index is exactly the current length (the next free index). Assignment to an existing index replaces that entry. Assignment past the end (an index greater than the length) is an error; Adaptive Script does not fill missing indexes with undefined on assign.

create_array(n) creates a new mutable array of length n whose entries are all undefined. The length must be a non-negative integer within the implementation limit documented for that function in the Function Reference. Use it when you want a known length up front; use push or assignment at the next free index when growing as you go. This is a length-based constructor, not a conversion function. array(...) builds from elements (and optional spread); a non-spread array argument is nested as one element. Spreading a string gives its code points: [..."ab"] is ["a", "b"]. Write that where a function needs an array and you have a string: map([..."ab"], f). Only join, any_of and all_of accept a string directly.
A second argument to create_array fills every entry with that value instead of undefined.

An array can hold values of any data type. If you would like an array that only ever holds one, make a typed array with array<T>(…): every value must be a T, now and later, so push of a string onto an array<integer> is an error.

splice(array, startIndex, deleteCount?, …values) removes zero or more values starting at startIndex and optionally inserts new values there. It returns an array of the removed values. Negative startIndex counts from the end. If deleteCount is omitted, all values from the start index through the end are removed.
freeze(value) makes an object or array immutable so further mutation throws. Freezing an already immutable value is a no-op. The same value is returned.

You do not need clone just to change an object or array you were given. An object or array literal gives you a fresh value each time it is evaluated, so a change made in one call of a function is not there the next time. An object from get_object or retrieve_objects can be changed too; the change stays in your copy until you save it with modify_object, replace_object, or update_object. Use clone when you want a deep, independent copy of a whole value, and freeze when nothing should change it. const only keeps the name from being assigned again; the value it names can still change unless it is frozen.

section.header: Walking an array with a function
section.paragraph: map, filter, find, find_index, some, every and reduce take the array first and a function second, so the method form chains: a->filter(p)->map(f). A script function is called with (value, index, array) (reduce: (accumulator, value, index, array)) and ignores the arguments it does not declare. A built-in function is called with the value alone, so map(a, to_string) works and map(a, add<integer>) is an error rather than quietly adding the index.

reduce(array, fn, initialValue?) starts with the first entry when there is no initial value; an empty array with no initial value is an error. A string is not walked: write [...s] for its code points.

Use all_of / any_of (function first, XACML's order, with extra values passed on every call) when you already rely on that naming or need the wider quantifier family documented under higher-order array functions.

sort(array, compareFn?) and reverse(array) change the array and return it. compareFn returns a boolean (true when its first argument comes first) or an integer (negative when it comes first). With no compareFn, values are ordered as < orders them, not converted to strings, and a mix of data types is an error. undefined entries go last. The sort is stable.
to_sorted, to_reversed, to_spliced and with_at return a changed copy and leave the array alone.
A few more functions round out everyday array work:

list.item: concat(a, b, …) joins arrays into a new one. Every argument is an array; to add one value, write [...a, v].
includes(a, v, fromIndex?), index_of(a, v, fromIndex?), and last_index_of find a value by equality, so an equal array or object is found too.
flat(a, depth?) flattens nested arrays one level, or depth levels (-1 for all of them), and flat_map(a, fn) maps and then flattens one level.
find_last and find_last_index search from the end, and reduce_right reduces from the end.
fill(a, v, start?, end?) sets entries to a value in place.
group_by(a, fn) makes an object whose properties are the names fn returns, each holding the values that got that name.
from_entries(e) is the opposite of entries: it makes an object from [name, value] pairs.

doc.paragraph: A string is a sequence of Unicode code points, and in many places you can walk it the way you walk an array. Each code point is one step, whatever the language: an é or an emoji is a single character, never two halves.

The string functions count the same way. slice(s, start, end?) and substring(s, start, end?) return a string; slice counts a negative index from the end, and substring treats one as zero, so substring("abc", 1, -1) is "a". split keeps empty pieces, so split("a,", ",") is ["a", ""], and replace with an empty search string puts the replacement between every character: replace("abc", "", "x", -1) is "xaxbxcx".

Functions that work on arrays, such as map and filter, do not take a string in place of an array. When you want to work on the characters, spread the string into an array first: map([...s], f). join, any_of, and all_of are the exceptions, and read a string as its code points.

Every string is kept in Unicode Normalization Form C, so text that looks the same is the same: an e followed by a combining accent is equal to a precomposed é, wherever each came from. A string never holds U+FEFF, the byte order mark; it is dropped when the string is made.
for (let x of array) walks array values in order, and for (let c of string) walks code points. Objects are not for-of iterable as a whole; iterate keys, values, or entries instead.

Function Reference categories: object, array, higher_order_array, and polymorphic methods (length, clone, freeze, and others). See also Language Features and Qualified Variables for additional language and host-context material.
